# Getting Water to the 30th Floor: How City Water Systems Maintain Pressure

If you've ever stood in a shower on the 25th floor of an apartment building and wondered why the water comes out with satisfying force, you've witnessed the quiet triumph of hydraulic engineering. The journey from a reservoir to that showerhead involves a careful interplay of gravity, pumps, tanks, and valves—and a surprising amount of deliberate planning about something as mundane as elevation.

## The Fundamental Physics: Elevation Is Everything

Water pressure in a municipal system is usually measured in pounds per square inch (psi), and the first thing an engineer will tell you is that pressure and height are two ways of describing the same thing. Every 2.31 feet of elevation gain costs you 1 psi. This conversion factor falls directly out of the physics: a column of water one foot square and 2.31 feet tall weighs exactly one pound per square inch at its base.

This simple relationship dominates everything else. Consider a hypothetical city—call it Riverbend—that draws its water from a reservoir in hills 300 feet above the downtown area.
